### Problem: Minimum Cost to Make Array Equal {#sec-srt-p5-b}

::: {.p-statement}
Two arrays `nums` and `cost` of the same length $n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$), with $\mathit{nums}[i], \mathit{cost}[i] \ge 1$ and at most $10^6$ each. Changing `nums[i]` by $1$ costs $\mathit{cost}[i]$ per unit. Make all elements **equal** with minimum total cost; the answer fits in $2^{53}-1$.

Source: [LC 2448 · Minimum Cost to Make Array Equal](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-cost-to-make-array-equal/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}

Example: `nums = [1,3,5,2], cost = [2,3,1,14]` → $8$ (gather at $2$: $2\cdot1 + 3\cdot1 + 1\cdot3 + 14\cdot0 = 8$). `nums = [2,2,2,2,2], cost = [4,2,8,1,3]` → $0$.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Same objective as @sec-srt-p5-a with one twist: each stick now has a *price tag*. Gathering to $t$ costs $f(t) = \sum_i \mathit{cost}_i \cdot |\mathit{nums}_i - t|$. The exchange argument survives verbatim if you imagine each pair $(\mathit{nums}_i, \mathit{cost}_i)$ as $\mathit{cost}_i$ **clones of a unit-cost stick sitting at** $\mathit{nums}_i$: moving the target one step right changes $f$ by (weight at-or-left) $-$ (weight strictly right). The turn happens where the weight stops being a majority on either side — the **weighted median**: sorting by `nums` and walking cumulative `cost`, the first position where the running weight reaches $\lceil \mathit{total}/2 \rceil$. That crossing point is always one of the `nums` values, so the walk never has to interpolate.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every candidate target.** The same slope argument says an optimal target is one of the `nums` values; for each distinct $t$ compute $\sum_i \mathit{cost}_i |\mathit{nums}_i - t|$ and keep the minimum. $O(n \cdot |\text{distinct}|)$ — the oracle.
2. **Sort + weighted prefix sums, evaluate cost at every value in $O(1)$.** Sort pairs by `nums`; build two tables — $\mathit{pref}_w$ (running weight) and $\mathit{pref}_{ws}$ (running $\mathit{nums} \cdot \mathit{cost}$). For target $v = \mathit{pairs}[i].\mathit{nums}$ the cost is $v \cdot \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]$ on the left plus $(\mathit{pref}_{ws}[n] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]) - v \cdot (\mathit{pref}_w[n] - \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1])$ on the right. Take the min. $O(n\log n)$ total.
3. **Sort by nums, stop at the weighted median.** Sort the pairs by value; walk them accumulating `cost`. The first value where $2 \cdot \mathit{cum} \ge \mathit{total}$ is the target; answer $= \sum_i \mathit{cost}_i |\mathit{nums}_i - t|$. $O(n\log n)$ time.

**Invariant.** Scanning pairs sorted by $\mathit{nums}$ with `cum` $= \sum_{j \le i} \mathit{cost}_j$: before $2 \cdot \mathit{cum} \ge \mathit{total}$ strictly more weight sits to the right of the current value, so $f$ still decreases when the target moves right; after passing it, at least half the weight sits at-or-left and $f$ never decreases again. The crossing value is therefore a minimiser.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Try every candidate target

::: {.form-next}
Reuse the definition of the cost directly: every distinct value is a candidate gathering point, and for each we pay $\mathit{cost}_i$ per unit distance for every element. $O(n^2)$ worst case — too slow at $n = 10^5$, kept as the oracle and as proof that the weighted median is not just folklore.

**Worked example.** `nums = [1,3,5,2]`, `cost = [2,3,1,14]`. $t=1: 2\cdot0 + 3\cdot2 + 1\cdot4 + 14\cdot1 = 24$; $t=2: 2\cdot1 + 3\cdot1 + 1\cdot3 + 14\cdot0 = 8$; $t=3: 2\cdot2 + 3\cdot0 + 1\cdot2 + 14\cdot1 = 20$; $t=5: 2\cdot4 + 3\cdot2 + 1\cdot0 + 14\cdot3 = 56$. Best $t=2$, cost $8$ — LC's answer.
:::


::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def cost_brute(nums, cost):
    best = math.inf
    for t in set(nums):
        best = min(best, sum(c * abs(x - t) for x, c in zip(nums, cost)))
    return best
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - try every distinct value as target (oracle)
#include <vector>
#include <set>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
ll costBrute(vector<ll> nums, vector<ll> cost) {
    set<ll> cand(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    ll best = (ll)4e18;
    for (ll t : cand) {
        ll c = 0;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < nums.size(); ++i) c += cost[i] * abs(nums[i] - t);
        best = min(best, c);
    }
    return best;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `for t in set(nums)` enumerates only the *present* values — the slope of $f$ changes exactly there, so an optimum is among them. `sum(c * abs(x - t) for x, c in zip(nums, cost))` evaluates the objective literally, each pair's distance priced by its own `cost`. `math.inf` / `4e18` are sentinels larger than any answer; LC only promises the answer is at most $2^{53}-1 \approx 9 \cdot 10^{15}$, so 64-bit ints throughout — `int` overflows past $2^{31}-1 \approx 2.1 \cdot 10^9$.

#### Sort + weighted prefix sums, evaluate every value in $O(1)$

::: {.form-next}
Just like @sec-srt-p5-a's prefix rung, but with two tables instead of one: $\mathit{pref}_w$ accumulates the weights, $\mathit{pref}_{ws}$ accumulates $\mathit{nums} \cdot \mathit{cost}$. Once both tables exist, every candidate target's cost is four multiplications and two subtractions. Try all $n$ values, keep the min. $O(n\log n)$ total (sort dominates), and **no weighted-median insight is required** — the machinery answers by enumeration, so this rung is a legitimate intermediate between the $O(n^2)$ brute and the $O(n\log n)$ one-line median walk. Same asymptotics as the median form, but a longer code and an extra table.

**Weighted prefix sums, in plain words.** Sort pairs $(v, c)$ by $v$. $\mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1] = c_0 + \dots + c_i$ is the total weight up to (and including) index $i$, and $\mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1] = v_0 c_0 + \dots + v_i c_i$ is the running weighted sum. For target $t = v_i$: the left side $\sum_{j \le i} c_j (v_i - v_j)$ is $v_i \cdot \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]$; the right side $\sum_{j > i} c_j (v_j - v_i)$ is $(\mathit{pref}_{ws}[n] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]) - v_i \cdot (\mathit{pref}_w[n] - \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1])$. Add them for the total cost.

**Worked example.** Pairs sorted by value: $(1,2), (2,14), (3,3), (5,1)$. $\mathit{pref}_w = [0, 2, 16, 19, 20]$; $\mathit{pref}_{ws} = [0, 2, 30, 39, 44]$. At $v = 1$: $\mathit{lc} = 1 \cdot 2 - 2 = 0$, $\mathit{rc} = (44-2) - 1 \cdot 18 = 24$, cost $24$. At $v = 2$: $\mathit{lc} = 2 \cdot 16 - 30 = 2$, $\mathit{rc} = (44-30) - 2 \cdot 4 = 6$, cost $8$. At $v = 3$: $\mathit{lc} = 3 \cdot 19 - 39 = 18$, $\mathit{rc} = (44-39) - 3 \cdot 1 = 2$, cost $20$. At $v = 5$: $\mathit{lc} = 5 \cdot 20 - 44 = 56$, $\mathit{rc} = 0$, cost $56$. Minimum $= 8$, at $v = 2$ — matching LC's answer.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-2448-prefix
def cost_prefix(nums, cost):
    pairs = sorted(zip(nums, cost))
    n = len(pairs)
    pref_w, pref_ws = [0], [0]
    for v, c in pairs:
        pref_w.append(pref_w[-1] + c)
        pref_ws.append(pref_ws[-1] + c * v)
    best = math.inf
    for i, (v, _) in enumerate(pairs):
        lc = v * pref_w[i + 1] - pref_ws[i + 1]
        rc = (pref_ws[n] - pref_ws[i + 1]) - v * (pref_w[n] - pref_w[i + 1])
        best = min(best, lc + rc)
    return best

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 10)
    nums = [random.randint(1, 15) for _ in range(n)]
    cost = [random.randint(1, 10) for _ in range(n)]
    assert cost_prefix(nums, cost) == cost_brute(nums, cost)
assert cost_prefix([1, 3, 5, 2], [2, 3, 1, 14]) == 8
print("cost_prefix OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
using ll = long long;

ll minCostPrefix(vector<int> nums, vector<int> cost) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<pair<ll, ll>> pairs;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) pairs.push_back({nums[i], cost[i]});
    sort(pairs.begin(), pairs.end());
    vector<ll> pw(n + 1, 0), pws(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        pw[i + 1] = pw[i] + pairs[i].second;
        pws[i + 1] = pws[i] + pairs[i].first * pairs[i].second;
    }
    ll best = (ll)4e18;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        ll v = pairs[i].first;
        ll lc = v * pw[i + 1] - pws[i + 1];
        ll rc = (pws[n] - pws[i + 1]) - v * (pw[n] - pw[i + 1]);
        best = min(best, lc + rc);
    }
    return best;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> a{1, 3, 5, 2}, b{2, 3, 1, 14};
    cout << minCostPrefix(a, b) << '\n';
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `pairs = sorted(zip(nums, cost))` is the same value-ordered pairing @sec-srt-p5-a uses; here each row carries its price. Two prefix tables run in lockstep: `pref_w` totals weights, `pref_ws` totals $v \cdot c$. For target $t = v_i$, `lc` computes the sum of $c_j \cdot (v_i - v_j)$ over $j \le i$ — distributively, $v_i \cdot \mathit{pref}_w[i{+}1] - \mathit{pref}_{ws}[i{+}1]$ — and `rc` mirrors it on the right. Same $O(n\log n)$ asymptotics as the median form below, but two tables and $n$ evaluations instead of one walk and one final sum. Every accumulator is `ll` — with $n = 10^5$ and values up to $10^6$, both $\mathit{pref}_w$ and the answer can pass $2^{31}$.

#### Sort by nums, stop at the weighted median

::: {.form-next}
The Hard-problem prize in five lines: sort the pairs by value, accumulate weights, stop where the running weight reaches half the total, then sum deviations to that target. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

**Weighted median, in plain words.** A weight is how loud a value shouts in the cost. Lined up by value, the cost-minimising target is where the crowd on either side can no longer outvote the other: the first value whose cumulative weight (from the left) is at least half of all weight. With every weight equal to $1$ this is exactly the ordinary median of @sec-srt-p5-a — nothing new is proved, only counted with prices attached.

**Worked example.** Pairs sorted by `nums`: $(1,2), (2,14), (3,3), (5,1)$; total weight $20$. Running cum: $2, 16, 19, 20$. The first with $2 \cdot \mathit{cum} \ge 20$ is the value $2$ (cum $16$). Cost $= 2\cdot1 + 14\cdot0 + 3\cdot1 + 1\cdot3 = 8$ — matches the oracle.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-2448-median
def cost_median(nums, cost):
    pairs = sorted(zip(nums, cost))
    total = sum(c for _, c in pairs)
    cum, target = 0, pairs[-1][0]
    for x, c in pairs:
        cum += c
        if 2 * cum >= total:          # weight majority reached
            target = x
            break
    return sum(c * abs(x - target) for x, c in pairs)

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 10)
    nums = [random.randint(1, 15) for _ in range(n)]
    cost = [random.randint(1, 10) for _ in range(n)]
    assert cost_median(nums, cost) == cost_brute(nums, cost)
assert cost_median([1, 3, 5, 2], [2, 3, 1, 14]) == 8       # LC example; the board sample
assert cost_median([2, 2, 2, 2, 2], [4, 2, 8, 1, 3]) == 0  # already equal
assert cost_median([5], [7]) == 0                           # single element
print("cost_median OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
using ll = long long;

ll minCost(vector<int> nums, vector<int> cost) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    vector<pair<ll, ll>> pairs;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) pairs.push_back({nums[i], cost[i]});
    sort(pairs.begin(), pairs.end());
    ll total = 0;
    for (auto& pr : pairs) total += pr.second;
    ll cum = 0, target = pairs.back().first;
    for (auto& pr : pairs) {
        cum += pr.second;
        if (2 * cum >= total) { target = pr.first; break; }
    }
    ll ans = 0;
    for (auto& pr : pairs) ans += pr.second * abs(pr.first - target);
    return ans;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> a{1, 3, 5, 2}, b{2, 3, 1, 14};
    cout << minCost(a, b) << '\n';
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `pairs = sorted(zip(nums, cost))` sorts *by value carrying its price along* — the "carry the payload with the value" habit from @sec-srt-a2. `total` is all the weight in the room. The walk `cum += c; if 2*cum >= total: target = x; break` is the vote count: `2*cum >= total` is integer-safe arithmetic for "cum has reached half". The final sum prices every deviation from `target` at its own rate. Every accumulator is `ll` — the answer can exceed $2^{31}$ even though inputs stay $\le 10^6$.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try every target** is $O(n \cdot |\text{distinct}|)$ time. **Sort + weighted prefix** is $O(n\log n)$ time (sort dominates; two tables and an $O(n)$ scan) and $O(n)$ space for the pairs plus two prefix vectors. **Weighted median** is $O(n\log n)$ time (sort dominates; the walk and final sum are $O(n)$) and $O(n)$ space, and collapses the whole computation to a single target evaluation once the majority-weight position is found. Compare with a *prefix-sum over values* solution, $O(V + n)$ with $V = 10^6$ — a counting-sort flavour (@sec-srt-p3-a) that trades $\log n$ for the value range; the median route is shorter to write and never cares how wide $V$ is.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All `nums` equal: every deviation is $0$, answer $0$ — the walk still lands on that value.
- Weights up to $10^6$ each and $n$ up to $10^5$: `total` reaches $10^{11}$ and the answer may reach the promised bound $2^{53}-1$ — 64-bit is mandatory.
- The break condition uses $2 \cdot \mathit{cum} \ge \mathit{total}$, not `cum >= total/2`, to avoid float and floor-division off-by-one on odd totals.
:::
